content: Patient engagement, also referred to as patient activation or patient participation, is defined as the involvement of patients in the decision-making process regarding their health. Patients may have the ability to identify errors in medical documentation. Patient activation can be assessed using the Patient Activation Measure. Readiness to change can be evaluated through various methods, including the Readiness to Change Ruler and Prochaska's Stages of Change from the Transtheoretical Model of Change. Subjects are asked to respond to statements reflecting their current beliefs, such as: I do not regularly use [behavior/intervention] and do not intend to start within the next six months (Precontemplation). I am considering using [behavior/intervention] regularly within the next six months (Contemplation). I plan to use [behavior/intervention] regularly within the next 30 days (Preparation). I use [behavior/intervention] regularly and have been doing so for less than six months (Action). I use [behavior/intervention] regularly and have been doing so for six months or more (Maintenance). The University of Rhode Island Change Assessment (URICA) questionnaire, based on the Transtheoretical Model of Change, is another tool for measuring readiness to change. It consists of 23 or 32 items, with a shorter 12-item Readiness to Change version also available. The Readiness to Change Ruler correlates with the full questionnaire and predicts behavioral intentions. Motivational interviewing, as developed by Rollnick, is another approach to enhance patient engagement. Several strategies have been reviewed to increase patient engagement and participation. For example, using narratives or stories to convey medical evidence can improve communication. Encouraging patients to actively participate in decision-making processes can enhance their engagement and adherence to treatment plans. The design of consultation rooms can also play a role. Structuring the room so that patients can observe healthcare providers entering information into electronic health records may foster engagement. Patient portals linked to electronic health records can increase patient activation and facilitate the reporting of errors. Test results can be released directly to patients in real time, without requiring interpretation by healthcare providers.
